title: Hand of Straights
directAnswer: Decide whether the hand can be split into groups of `groupSize` consecutive cards. The brute force repeatedly sorts and peels a run off the front in O(n² log n). The greedy is forced, not clever: count the cards, then always start the next group at the smallest remaining card and consume `groupSize` consecutive values from it — there is no smaller card to absorb the minimum, so it must lead a group. With a TreeMap (Java) or a heap + hash map (Python) that's O(n log n) time.

remember.pattern: Greedy 'smallest card must lead a group' + ordered counts
remember.formula:
if len(hand) % groupSize: return False
count = Counter(hand)
while count:
    start = min(remaining keys)        # heap / TreeMap gives this in O(log n)
    for c in range(start, start + groupSize):
        if count[c] == 0: return False
        count[c] -= 1
return True
rules: Fail fast: if `len(hand) % groupSize != 0` the split is impossible — return `False` before doing any work.
The **smallest remaining card** has no smaller neighbour, so it **must** be the start of a group — this is forced, the heart of the greedy.
From that smallest card, consume exactly `groupSize` **consecutive** values; a missing value mid-run means failure.
Use an **ordered structure** for 'give me the current minimum fast': `TreeMap` in Java, a **min-heap of keys + hash map of counts** in Python.
Decrement counts, not a list — duplicates of the same card belong to **different** groups, so never dedupe them away.
Only pop the minimum from the heap when its count hits **zero**, and only if it really is the current minimum — otherwise a smaller card was orphaned.
whenToUse: Partition a multiset into runs of consecutive (or fixed-step) values
An element's smallest member is forced to anchor its group
You repeatedly need the current minimum among remaining counts
Counts of duplicates matter and groups are size-fixed
antiSignals: Groups need not be consecutive (arbitrary subsets) → this forced-anchor logic doesn't apply
Order within a group is free and values can repeat freely → it's a counting/parity problem, not a run partition
You must output the actual groups under tight memory → still doable but watch the bookkeeping
Group size varies per group → the fixed-window consume breaks
remember.takeaway: Hand of Straights is the cleanest 'the minimum is forced to anchor a group' greedy: because nothing is smaller than the current minimum, it has no choice but to lead, which removes all decision-making. The same forced-anchor idea drives Divide Array in Sets of K Consecutive Numbers — recognise it whenever a multiset must break into consecutive runs.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you spot that the smallest remaining card is *forced* to begin a group (so there's no search, just bookkeeping), and whether you pick the right data structure to fetch the running minimum and decrement duplicate counts efficiently.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to backtrack over which cards join which group as if there's a choice, or de-duplicating the hand and losing the count of repeated cards so two groups that need the same value collide.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the forced-anchor argument out loud — 'the minimum can't sit in the middle or end of any consecutive run, so it must lead one' — then pick a TreeMap / heap to make 'smallest remaining' O(log n) and note the len % groupSize early-out.

problemStatement:
Alice has some number of cards and she wants to rearrange the cards into groups so that each group is of size `groupSize`, and consists of `groupSize` **consecutive** cards.

Given an integer array `hand` where `hand[i]` is the value written on the `i`-th card and an integer `groupSize`, return `true` if she can rearrange the cards, or `false` otherwise.
constraints: Each group must be groupSize consecutive integers (e.g. [3,4,5])
understanding: You hold a multiset of card values. Partition every card into groups of exactly groupSize, where each group is a run of consecutive integers like [v, v+1, …, v+groupSize−1]. Every card must be used exactly once. Return whether such a partition exists — not the groups themselves.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must every card be used, or can some be left over?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Every card must belong to exactly one group. That's why len(hand) must be divisible by groupSize, or it's immediately impossible.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the hand contain duplicate values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — duplicates go into different groups. Two 4s mean two separate runs each need a 4, so we track counts, never dedupe.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does 'consecutive' mean strictly +1 steps?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, a group is v, v+1, …, v+groupSize−1. No gaps, no repeats within one group.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if groupSize is 1?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Every single card is its own trivial group, so the answer is always true. The algorithm handles it naturally — each card consumes a run of length 1.

examples.explanation: Groups [1,2,3], [2,3,4], [6,7,8]. The smallest card 1 leads the first group, forcing 2 and 3 along with it.
5 cards can't be split into groups of 4 (5 % 4 ≠ 0) — fails the divisibility check before any grouping.
Smallest is 8, which forces a group [8, 9, 10], but there's no 9 — so no valid partition exists.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Once you see the minimum is forced to anchor a group, the only question is how fast you can fetch that minimum.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Sort, Then Peel a Run Off the Front
approaches.whenToMention: Lead here to establish the forced-anchor idea concretely, then call out that re-finding the minimum by re-sorting (or scanning) is the wasteful part to optimise.
hints: Sort the cards. The smallest card has nothing smaller to pair with, so it must start a group. What group is it forced into?
Remove a run of groupSize consecutive values starting at that smallest card. If any value in the run is missing, fail.
Repeat: find the new smallest remaining card and peel another run. Keep going until the hand is empty or a run can't be completed.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of up to n/groupSize rounds finds the current minimum and removes a run; if you re-sort or rescan a list of size O(n) each round, that's O(n) per round across O(n) rounds with sorting overhead — O(n² log n) in the naive form.
approaches.explanation:
Sort the hand, then repeatedly take the smallest remaining card, claim a run of `groupSize` consecutive values starting there, and remove those cards. If a needed value is absent, the partition is impossible.

**Why the smallest card anchors a group — the core observation.** Consider the minimum value `m` still in the hand. In any valid partition, `m` lives in some group, and that group is a run of consecutive integers. `m` cannot be the *second-or-later* element of its run, because that would require `m − 1` to also be present and unused — but `m` is the smallest card left, so nothing smaller exists. Therefore `m` is *forced* to be the **first** element of its group. There is no decision to make: the group containing `m` must be exactly `[m, m+1, …, m+groupSize−1]`.

**Why peeling that exact run is safe.** Since the group for `m` is forced, removing `[m, …, m+groupSize−1]` can never be a mistake — we're not choosing among options, we're executing the only legal move. After removal, the new minimum of what remains is again forced to anchor its own group, and the argument repeats. This is what makes the greedy *exact*: every step is mandatory, so there's nothing to backtrack over.

**Why this implementation is slow.** Conceptually the algorithm is perfect; the naive realisation is wasteful. Sorting once is `O(n log n)`, but if each round re-sorts or linearly scans a remaining list to find and delete the next minimum and its run, you pay `O(n)` (or worse) per round across `O(n)` rounds — landing around `O(n² log n)` with list deletions. The logic is right; the bookkeeping needs a better data structure.

**Why we keep the idea but change the container.** Nothing about the forced-anchor argument changes — we just need 'give me the current minimum' and 'decrement a card's count' to each be cheap. That's exactly what a `TreeMap` (ordered keys) or a min-heap of distinct values plus a hash map of counts provides, dropping the cost to `O(n log n)`.
approaches.insight: The whole problem has *zero* search: the minimum is always forced to lead a group, so there's never a choice to explore or undo. Recognising 'forced move' versus 'genuine choice' is the difference between an exponential backtracking attempt and a clean linear-ish greedy. The only engineering question left is how fast you can serve the running minimum.

dryRun.intro: Sort to [1,2,2,3,3,4,6,7,8]. Repeatedly peel a 3-run starting at the smallest remaining card.

java.explanation: Indivisible total can never partition into equal groups — cheapest early-out.
TreeMap.firstKey() is the smallest remaining card — the forced anchor.
A consecutive value is missing → the forced group can't be completed.
Consume one copy of this card; remove the key only when its count hits zero.

python.explanation: Divisibility gate before any grouping work.
Visit candidate anchors in ascending order — the smallest unused card leads.
Duplicates of the anchor each start their own group, so loop while copies remain.
Missing consecutive value → impossible, return False.

pitfalls: De-duplicating the hand and losing duplicate counts — two groups needing the same value then collide.
Re-sorting the whole remaining list every round instead of using an ordered structure.
Skipping the len % groupSize check and discovering infeasibility only after wasted work.

approaches.name: Greedy — Forced Anchor via Heap + Count Map (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'the minimum is forced to lead a group, I just need O(log n) access to that minimum' — TreeMap in Java, heap + counts in Python.
hints: Keep the forced-anchor insight: the smallest remaining card must start a group. The only thing to optimise is fetching that smallest card repeatedly.
Use a hash map for counts and a min-heap of the distinct card values. The heap top is always the current smallest card.
Take the heap's minimum, consume groupSize consecutive values by decrementing counts. When a card's count hits zero, it must be the current heap minimum to pop — if a smaller card is orphaned, fail.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the count map is O(n) and heapifying distinct keys is O(n). Each card is consumed once, and heap pops/peeks cost O(log n), so total work is O(n log n) time; the map and heap hold up to n entries → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Build a count map `value → frequency` and a min-heap of the distinct values. While the heap is non-empty, peek the minimum `first` — the forced anchor — and consume `groupSize` consecutive values `first, first+1, …, first+groupSize−1`, decrementing each count. If any required value is absent (count zero), return `false`. When a card's count reaches zero, it must be the current heap minimum for us to pop it; if it isn't, a smaller card has been stranded and we fail.

**Why the heap, not just sorting once.** The forced-anchor argument says we always need the *current* smallest remaining card, and 'remaining' shrinks unevenly as duplicates get consumed at different rates. A heap (or `TreeMap`) gives that running minimum in `O(log n)` without re-sorting. Each of the `n` cards is consumed exactly once, and we touch the heap a logarithmic amount per distinct value, so the whole thing is `O(n log n)`.

**Why the 'count hit zero must be the min' check is the subtle correctness guard.** We always consume runs starting from the global minimum. Suppose while filling a run we decrement some card `c` to zero, but `c` is *not* currently the smallest value in the heap — meaning some value `d < c` still has a positive count. That `d` was skipped: it should have anchored its own group *before* we ever consumed `c`, yet here it sits with cards left while `c` is exhausted. No future group can ever include `d` (every later anchor is `≥` the current `first ≥ d`, and a run starting at `≥ first` that reaches `d` would need `d` to be in the *middle* of a run, impossible since `d` is below the anchor). So `d` is orphaned and the answer is `false`. Detecting 'a card emptied out of order' is exactly that orphan check.

**Why this greedy is provably optimal — the exchange/contradiction argument.** Claim: if any valid partition exists, the forced-anchor greedy finds one. Suppose, for contradiction, the greedy fails on a hand that *does* admit a valid partition `P`. Look at the first step where greedy claims the run `[m, …, m+groupSize−1]` for the minimum `m`. In `P`, the card `m` also lives in some group, and as argued `m` must be the first element of that group — so `P`'s group for `m` is *also* `[m, …, m+groupSize−1]`, identical to greedy's choice. Thus greedy's move matches a valid partition exactly; remove that group from both and the same argument applies to the new minimum, by induction. So greedy never diverges from *some* valid partition, contradicting the assumption that it fails where one exists. The 'no choice for the minimum' fact is what makes the exchange trivial: there's only one legal group for the smallest card, so greedy and the optimal solution are forced into the same first move.

**Why this beats the brute force.** Same forced-anchor logic, but 'fetch the minimum' drops from an `O(n)` rescan to an `O(log n)` heap op, collapsing `O(n² log n)` to `O(n log n)` while keeping `O(n)` space for the counts.
approaches.insight: The greedy is correct precisely because there is *no* greedy choice — the minimum has a single legal home, so 'greedy' and 'optimal' make the identical move at every step. When you can prove a step is forced (not merely locally attractive), you get an exact algorithm for free and skip the usual exchange-argument gymnastics. The only craft left is serving the running minimum cheaply: heap or TreeMap.

dryRun.intro: count = {1:1,2:2,3:2,4:1,6:1,7:1,8:1}; heap of keys. Peek min, consume a 3-run, pop emptied keys in order.

java.explanation: Indivisible total → impossible before any grouping.
Build value → frequency; TreeMap keeps keys ordered so the minimum is O(log n).
Smallest remaining card — the forced anchor of the next group.
A consecutive value is gone → the forced run can't complete.
Consume one copy; drop the key when its count reaches zero so firstKey() stays correct.

python.explanation: value → frequency; duplicates kept as counts, never deduped away.
Distinct values in a min-heap so the smallest remaining card is the heap top.
Peek the current minimum — the forced group anchor.
Required consecutive value exhausted → no valid partition.
A card emptied out of order means a smaller card was orphaned — fail.
Remove the now-empty minimum so the next peek is the new smallest.

diagrams.title: Why the minimum is forced to lead
diagrams.caption: The smallest remaining card has no smaller neighbour, so it can only be the first element of its run — there's no choice to search.

edgeCases.behavior: count {1:2,2:2,3:2}; min 1 → consume 1,2,3 (counts→1,1,1); 1 still positive so re-anchor at 1 → consume 1,2,3 → all empty → true (two groups [1,2,3]).
min 1 → consume 1,2; min 4 → consume 4,5 → true. Two runs of length 2.
min 8 → needs 8,9,10 but count[9]==0 → return false.

pitfalls: Popping a card from the heap when its count hits zero without confirming it's the current minimum — masks an orphaned smaller card.
Using count[card] without ensuring the key exists (in Java, treating a null Integer as 0) — NullPointerException.
Forgetting that an anchor with count > 1 must start multiple groups — loop while its count remains positive.

commonMistakes: Treating group assignment as a search/backtracking problem when the minimum's group is fully forced.
De-duplicating the hand and losing duplicate counts, so two groups needing the same value collide.
Re-sorting or rescanning the whole remaining hand each round instead of using a TreeMap or heap for the running minimum.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Losing duplicate counts by deduping
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Two cards of value 2 belong to two different groups. Storing values in a set instead of counting frequencies makes the second group silently miss its 2.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
count = Counter(hand)         # keeps how many of each value
# consume by decrementing count[card], removing only at zero

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Popping the heap minimum out of order
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When a card empties but isn't the current minimum, a smaller card was skipped and can never be placed. Popping it anyway hides that orphan and returns a false true.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if count[card] == 0:
    heapq.heappop(min_heap)   # pops regardless of position

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping the divisibility early-out
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If len(hand) isn't a multiple of groupSize, no partition can exist; without this guard you do full work and may even return a wrong answer on edge inputs.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
TreeMap<Integer,Integer> count = new TreeMap<>();
// ... build and group without checking divisibility

patternNote: Canonical 'forced anchor' greedy: the smallest remaining element must lead its group, so there is no choice to search — only fast access to the running minimum (TreeMap or heap + count map). Recognise it for partitioning a multiset into consecutive runs; it's the same engine as Divide Array in Sets of K Consecutive Numbers.
